note: Historical database of major US financial crises/bubbles. 'Buildup period' covers the 5-15 years before the trigger. Distributional consequences documented where evidence exists. Analysis of the preceding era, not just the visible administration (root Section 6).

crises.name: Panic of 1907
crises.buildup: Rapid industrialization, trust concentration, unregulated trust companies using depositor funds for speculation; San Francisco earthquake 1906 insurance payouts tightened liquidity; prior panics 1893, 1901.
crises.credit_conditions: Free banking era; no central bank; no deposit insurance
crises.monetary_policy: None (no central bank); J.P. Morgan private rescue
crises.trigger: Run on Knickerbocker Trust (Oct 1907); margin-call cascade
crises.response: Private lender-of-last-resort by Morgan syndicate; Aldrich-Vreeland Act 1908; Federal Reserve Act 1913
crises.distribution: Wealthy financiers (incl. Morgan) profited from rescue purchases; depositors of failed trusts lost savings; consolidation of banking power
crises.warning_indicators: Rising trust-company deposits, falling bank reserve ratios, prior 1901 panic
crises.lessons: Without a lender of last resort, panics recur; the Fed was the institutional response

crises.name: 1929 Crash & Great Depression
crises.buildup: Roaring Twenties: margin lending (~90% margin debt growth 1926-29), holding-company pyramids, utilities speculation, farmland boom then bust (1920s), weak bank regulation, no Fed response culture; Coolidge-era tax cuts and easy money; productivity boom.
crises.leverage: Extreme margin debt (brokers' loans >$8B, ~2x 1925); banks 8-12x capital
crises.credit_conditions: Easy money 1927-28 (Fed cut to support UK); then tightening 1928-29
crises.regulation: No SEC, no FDIC, no Glass-Steagall; wildcat banking
crises.monetary_policy: Fed raised rates 1928-29 (pop), then held contractionary through 1931-33 (gold standard; bank failures ~9,000)
crises.trigger: Oct 1929 crash (DJIA -23% in two days, Oct 28-29); then bank runs 1930-33
crises.response: RFC (1932, Hoover); FDR: bank holiday, FDIC, SEC, Glass-Steagall, gold abandonment 1933; Social Security; massive public works; WWII eventually ended depression
crises.recovery: GDP back to 1929 level by 1936, then 1937-38 recession; full employment only with WWII (1941-43)
crises.distribution: Wealth destroyed across classes but recovery heavily favored owners of financial assets; New Deal safety net created; farm and homeowner relief; lasting distrust of banks
crises.warning_indicators: Margin debt records, valuation extremes (CAPE ~32 in 1929), housing/land bubbles, bank reserve erosion
crises.lessons: Leverage + weak regulation + contractionary policy amid deflation = depression; institutional response reshaped US finance for 50 years

crises.name: Savings & Loan Crisis
crises.visible_administration: Carter (seeds, DIDMCA 1980) / Reagan (deregulation 1981-82) / G.H.W. Bush (resolution, FIRREA 1989)
crises.buildup: S&Ls held long-term fixed mortgages funded by short deposits; 1970s inflation + 1980-81 Volcker rates created massive negative net worth; deregulation (DIDMCA 1980, Garn-St. Germain 1982) let them invest in commercial real estate, junk bonds, and growth strategies with insured deposits and thin capital.
crises.asset: Commercial real estate, junk bonds, direct investments
crises.leverage: High; capital requirements ~3-5%, often phantom (regulatory forbearance)
crises.credit_conditions: 1980s real-estate boom (tax shelter incentives, overbuilding); Southwest oil-bust 1986
crises.regulation: Deregulated asset powers; weak examiners; deposit insurance (FDIC/FSLIC) without risk pricing; 'too big to fail' brokered deposits
crises.monetary_policy: Volcker disinflation (1979-82) was the proximate shock; then low real rates fueled speculation
crises.trigger: 1986-87 commercial real estate collapse + oil price crash; Texas S&L failures
crises.response: FSLIC insolvent 1987; FIRREA 1989 created RTC; ~$160B total cost (~3.2% of GDP; 1,000+ institutions resolved); criminal referrals for fraud
crises.distribution: Taxpayer-funded bailout of depositors; developers/insiders profited before failure; regional concentration (TX, CA, AZ); contributed to 1990-91 credit crunch recession
crises.warning_indicators: Negative tangible net worth masked by forbearance, brokered deposits growth, commercial real estate overbuilding, rapid asset growth
crises.lessons: Deposit insurance without capital discipline + deregulated risk-taking = moral hazard; regulators can't forbear their way out

crises.name: Black Monday (Oct 19, 1987)
crises.buildup: 5-year bull market (DJIA +~230% 1982-87); portfolio insurance hedging; program trading; leveraged buyout boom; rising rates mid-1987 (Bundesbank/Fed tightening; dollar decline)
crises.regulation: Post-1975 deregulation of commissions; limited circuit breakers
crises.trigger: Sell-off accelerated by portfolio insurance feedback loop; DJIA -22.6% in one day; S&P -20.5%
crises.response: Greenspan 'liquidity put' (Fed supplied liquidity, cut rates); pledged to back markets; circuit breakers introduced
crises.distribution: Equity owners (mostly upper-income) bore paper losses; recovered; no banking contagion (thanks to rapid response)
crises.warning_indicators: Concentrated derivative exposure, record leverage, valuation divergence
crises.lessons: Mechanical strategies (portfolio insurance) amplify crashes; central-bank liquidity response prevents systemic spread

crises.name: Dot-Com Bubble
crises.buildup: Internet revolution + telecom deregulation (Telecom Act 1996) + low rates + Y2K capex; venture capital/IPO mania; NASDAQ +~580% 1995-2000; telecom debt ~$1T; 'eyeballs' valuation; Greenspan 'irrational exuberance' warning 1996 ignored.
crises.leverage: Moderate equity leverage; high corporate debt in telecom; margin debt records
crises.regulation: Light touch; 1996 Telecom Act promoted competition (and overbuilding); capital gains tax cut 1997
crises.monetary_policy: Fed cautious tightening 1999-2000 (June 1999-2000 hikes); too late
crises.trigger: March 2000 NASDAQ peak; cash-burn reckoning; 2001 recession and 9/11
crises.response: Fed aggressive easing 2001 (6.5%→1.75%); 2001/2003 tax cuts; military spending; housing stimulus (low rates)
crises.recovery: NASDAQ -78% peak-trough (Mar 2000-Oct 2002); S&P -49%; NASDAQ took 15 years to recover
crises.distribution: ~$5T market cap destroyed (largely upper-income households' portfolios); telecom debt losses hit banks moderately; 401(k) retirement losses broad
crises.warning_indicators: CAPE ~44 (Dec 1999, record), price/sales absurdity, IPO underpricing, venture capital boom
crises.lessons: Easy money can fuel equity manias even without credit excess; cheap post-bust policy (low rates) helped seed the next bubble (housing)

crises.name: Housing Bubble & 2008 Financial Crisis (Global Financial Crisis)
crises.buildup: Bipartisan homeownership push (Clinton NIIA 1994; Bush 'ownership society'), Fed low rates 2001-04 (1% fed funds), Greenspan put, securitization (MBS/CDO), GSE expansion (Fannie/Freddie), subprime & Alt-A origination, ratings agency conflicts, 2004 SEC net-capital rule (leverage 12x→33x for brokers), mark-to-market opacity, global savings glut financing US deficits; leverage at investment banks ~30:1; household debt/GDP 60%→98%.
crises.asset: Residential real estate (Case-Shiller +~90% 2000-2006 national), mortgage-backed securities, CDOs
crises.leverage: Extreme: banks 25-35x; GSEs 20-30x; shadow banking (SIVs, ABCP)
crises.credit_conditions: NINJA loans, no-doc, teaser ARMs; underwriting collapse; securitization severed originator accountability
crises.regulation: Deregulation: GLB 1999 (repealed Glass-Steagall), CFMA 2000 (exempted OTC derivatives), SEC 2004 leverage rule, OCC preemption; no federal regulator for subprime lenders; Fed chose not to use supervisory authority
crises.monetary_policy: 1% fed funds 2003-04 (too low too long); slow to tighten 2004-06; 'Greenspan put' priced in
crises.trigger: 2006 house-price peak; 2007 subprime defaults; Aug 2007 ABCP freeze; Mar 2008 Bear Stearns; Sep 2008 Fannie/Freddie conservatorship, Lehman failure (Sep 15), AIG rescue, money-market 'breaking the buck'
crises.response: TARP ($700B; ~$430B deployed, recovered ~$440B incl. interest per Treasury), Fed facilities (QE1, swap lines), ARRA 2009 ($831B), auto rescue, Dodd-Frank 2010 (Volcker Rule, CFPB, stress tests, OTC clearing), Basel III; GSEs stayed in conservatorship
crises.recovery: Unemployment peaked 10% (Oct 2009); S&P -57% peak-trough; house prices -27% (national); recovery slowest since GD (median income didn't surpass 2007 until 2016; labor force participation fell structurally)
crises.distribution: ~$8-13T household wealth destroyed (over half from housing, concentrated in middle class); foreclosure wave ~9-10M households; banks bailed out, shareholders of Lehman/AIG wiped out; homeownership fell 69%→63%; wealth inequality rose (top recovered via equities); Occupy Wall Street; lasting distrust of elites
crises.warning_indicators: Subprime share of origination >20%, housing price/rent and price/income records, CDO issuance records, GSE leverage, current-account deficit 6% of GDP, negative real rates
crises.lessons: Credit excess + securitization opacity + deregulation + asset-price targeting = systemic crisis; 'financial innovation' can export risk beyond regulatory reach; the recovery's slowness redistributed wealth upward

crises.name: COVID-19 Market Crash
crises.buildup: Longest expansion; corporate debt record ($10T, BBB share ~50% of IG), leveraged loans, equity valuations elevated, passive flows; COVID-19 pandemic shock (external, non-financial origin)
crises.asset: Equities (S&P -34% in 5 weeks, fastest bear market in history), credit spreads (HY +10pp), oil (negative futures Apr 2020)
crises.leverage: High corporate leverage; dealer balance-sheet constraints; Treasury market dysfunction mid-March
crises.regulation: Post-2008 framework held up (banks well capitalized, stress tests worked)
crises.monetary_policy: Fed: emergency 150bp cut to 0% (Mar 15), unlimited QE, credit facilities (PMCCF/SMCCF, Main Street, MMLF), swap lines; fiscal: CARES $2.2T (PPP, stimulus checks, UI+$600)
crises.response: Unprecedented monetary + fiscal speed; PPP and enhanced UI prevented income collapse; real median income ROSE in 2020 due to transfers
crises.recovery: S&P +68% from March low by Jan 2021; GDP -2.8% (2020) then +5.8% (2021); unemployment 14.7% (Apr 2020) → 3.5% (Feb 2020) → recovery 2021-22
crises.distribution: Transfers disproportionately helped bottom half (2020 poverty fell); asset rebound concentrated gains among top decile; excess savings ~$2.1T (concentrated upper-income); supply disruptions → 2021-22 inflation
crises.warning_indicators: Corporate leverage records, equity valuations, but crisis was exogenous — timing not predictable
crises.lessons: Adequate bank capital (post-2008 reform) made the difference; massive fiscal transfers prevented depression but contributed (with supply shocks and energy war) to 2021-22 inflation

crises.name: 2023 Regional Banking Crisis
crises.buildup: Fastest rate hikes since 1980s (0→5.25-5.50% in 14 months) → duration losses on HTM bond portfolios; deposit flight to money-market funds; SVB's uninsured deposit share ~94%; social-media-driven runs
crises.asset: Treasuries/MBS held at amortized cost (HTM), venture deposits
crises.leverage: Moderate; but duration mismatch severe; unrealized losses on bank securities ~$1.7T (FDIC, 2022)
crises.regulation: Post-2018 S.2155 loosened stress-test and liquidity requirements for mid-size banks (tailored regulation); SVB exempt from some DFAST/LCR rules
crises.monetary_policy: Tightening cycle (the proximate cause of duration losses)
crises.response: FDIC systemic-risk exception (full depositor guarantee beyond $250k), Bank Term Funding Program (par-value HTM collateral), US banks borrowed ~$165B; Fed + Treasury backstop; First Republic sold to JPMorgan
crises.recovery: Contained in weeks; no contagion to large banks; credit conditions tightened mildly
crises.distribution: Depositors made whole (above insurance — first large use of systemic-risk exception); shareholders of failed banks wiped out; debate over moral hazard
crises.warning_indicators: HTM unrealized losses, uninsured-deposit concentration, duration mismatch, rapid deposit growth (SVB deposits +~2x in 2 years)
crises.lessons: Fast rate cycles expose duration risk even in 'safe' assets; regulatory tailoring created gaps; social-media deposit runs are faster than 2008-era

crises.name: Current Fragility Conditions (as of Aug 2026)
crises.buildup: 15-year bull market; CAPE ~41 (Aug 2026) — second-highest ever after 1999-2000's 44; AI-capital-expenditure concentration (magnificent-seven ~35% of S&P weight); corporate debt near records; federal debt ~100% of GDP (public) and rising; deficits ~6% of GDP; net interest $970B (3.2% of GDP) and doubling within a decade; commercial real estate stress (office); household leverage moderate but housing unaffordability at records; geopolitics (tariffs, Ukraine, Middle East); democracy indices at record lows (V-Dem 0.57).
crises.asset: AI/tech equities, Treasuries (fiscal), commercial real estate
crises.leverage: Federal leverage rising; corporate moderate-high; households moderate; shadow-banking/private credit growth (unregulated $2T+ private credit)
crises.credit_conditions: Fed on hold 3.50-3.75%; yields elevated; credit spreads tight (complacency)
crises.regulation: Rollback era (SEC, CFPB, FTC, FDIC changes); private credit largely unregulated; Basel III endgame paused
crises.monetary_policy: Holding pattern; inflation sticky ~3%; QT ongoing; fiscal-monetary mix tension
crises.trigger: None yet — this is a RISK assessment, not a crisis
crises.distribution: N/A (see financial fragility section of report)
crises.warning_indicators: CAPE ~41, concentration, private credit growth, fiscal trajectory, housing unaffordability, interest burden
crises.lessons: Historical analogues (1999, 2007) suggest elevated valuations + leverage + complacency precede corrections; timing is unpredictable; fiscal capacity to respond is thinner than 2008/2020 (debt 100% vs 40%/80% of GDP)
